title: Landlocked Countries: No Coastline
summary: What it means for a country to have no coastline, examples from different continents, and how these countries trade with the rest of the world.
poll: A country with no coastline cannot trade with the rest of the world.

versions.title: Countries With No Coast
versions.text:
Look at a map. Do you see a line around each land? Most lands touch the sea.

But some do not. Land sits all around them. We call them landlocked.

A landlocked land has no coastline at all. It has no port by the sea. No ship can sail right to it.

This makes trade hard. A landlocked land must move its goods by land first.

So these lands make a deal with a friend land. The friend land has a coast. It lets goods pass through its port.

Trucks and trains move the goods the rest of the way. At last, the goods reach a ship.

Trade can still work, even with no coastline. Lands like this live all over the world.

Glance at a map of the world. You will notice a line around each country. Most countries touch the sea along part of their border.

Yet a number of countries do not touch the sea at all. Land surrounds them completely on every side. We call a country like this landlocked.

A landlocked country has no coastline anywhere. It has no port of its own by the sea. Large cargo ships can never sail right to it, simply because it has no coast to sail toward.

Landlocked countries can be found on nearly every continent. Bolivia and Paraguay are landlocked in South America. Switzerland and Austria are landlocked in Europe, among tall mountains. Mongolia is landlocked in Asia, between two huge neighbors, Russia and China. Chad and Niger are landlocked deep inside Africa, far from any ocean.

In all, roughly 44 countries around the world are landlocked. They are found on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.

Being landlocked creates real problems for a country's economy. Large cargo ships need a coast to load and unload goods. Without one, a landlocked country must move its goods over land first, and this adds both time and cost.

So landlocked countries sign trade agreements with a coastal neighbor. The neighbor agrees to let goods pass through one of its ports on the way to the open sea.

Trucks, trains, and river boats then carry the goods the rest of the way, across the border, until they finally reach the sea. Switzerland, for example, ships cargo along the Rhine River to a busy port.

Trade can still move steadily this way, even for a country with no coastline of its own.

A landlocked country possesses no coastline anywhere along its border. It has no port of its own by the sea, so large cargo ships can never sail directly to it, simply because it has none to sail toward in the first place; every shipment must instead travel over land, or along an inland river, for part of its journey.

Landlocked countries exist on nearly every continent of the world. Bolivia and Paraguay are landlocked in South America, hemmed in by other nations on every side. Switzerland and Austria are landlocked in Europe, among tall mountains, along with more than a dozen smaller nations scattered further east. Mongolia is landlocked in Asia, wedged between two enormous neighbors, Russia and China. Chad, Niger, and Mali are landlocked deep inside Africa, hundreds of kilometers from any ocean. A rare few nations, such as Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan, are doubly landlocked, meaning every one of their neighbors is landlocked too, a coincidence found almost nowhere else.

In total, roughly 44 countries around the world are classified as landlocked, found on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, which has no permanent population or sovereign government at all.

Being landlocked creates real and lasting problems for a country's economy, since large cargo ships require a coast where they can safely load and unload goods, and without one, every item a landlocked country buys or sells must cross a neighbor's territory first, adding both time and considerable extra cost along the way.

So landlocked countries negotiate detailed transit agreements with a coastal neighbor, under which the neighbor allows goods to pass through one of its ports on the way to the open sea, while trucks, trains, and river boats carry the cargo the rest of the way across the border.

versions.title: Landlocked Countries: No Coastline
versions.text:
A careful examination of a map of the world reveals a boundary line surrounding each country, and most countries touch the sea along part of their border, at least to some degree.

Yet a surprising number of countries do not touch the sea at all, regardless of which direction one surveys across their entire national territory. Land surrounds them completely on every side, and we therefore designate a country like this as landlocked.

A landlocked country possesses no coastline anywhere along its border. It has no port of its own by the sea, so large cargo vessels can never sail directly to it, simply because it possesses none to sail toward in the first place; every shipment must instead traverse land, or an inland river system, for part of its journey before ever reaching open water.

Landlocked countries exist on nearly every continent of the world. Bolivia and Paraguay are landlocked in South America, hemmed in by other nations on every side. Switzerland and Austria are landlocked in Europe, among towering mountains, along with more than a dozen smaller nations distributed further east across the continent. Mongolia is landlocked in Asia, wedged tightly between two colossal neighbors, Russia and China. Chad, Niger, and Mali are landlocked deep within Africa, hundreds of kilometers removed from any ocean. A rare few nations, such as Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan, are classified as doubly landlocked, signifying that every single one of their neighbors is itself landlocked, a coincidence found almost nowhere else on the planet.

In total, approximately 44 countries worldwide are classified as landlocked, identifiable on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, the latter possessing no permanent population or sovereign government whatsoever.

Being landlocked imposes real and persistent challenges upon a country's economy, since large cargo vessels require a coast where they can safely load and unload goods, and in its absence, every commodity a landlocked country buys or sells must transit a neighbor's territory first, adding both time and considerable extra cost to the final price.

Landlocked countries therefore negotiate detailed transit agreements with a coastal neighbor, under which the neighbor formally permits goods to travel through one of its ports en route to the open sea, while trucks, trains, or river barges convey the cargo the remaining distance across the border.

Switzerland, for instance, ships much of its cargo along the Rhine River to the bustling port of Rotterdam, hundreds of kilometers distant, while Ethiopia relies upon a modern railway connecting it to a port on the Red Sea. Many landlocked nations also join regional trade organizations, which guarantee member countries a legal right to move goods through a neighbor's territory under agreed, predictable rules. Trade can thereby continue to flow steadily, even for a country that possesses no coastline of its own.

versions.title: Landlocked Countries: No Coastline
versions.text:
Across the continents of the world, a careful examination of a map reveals a boundary line surrounding each country, and most nations touch the sea along at least a portion of their border.

Yet a surprising number of countries, scattered across nearly every inhabited continent, do not touch the sea at all, regardless of which direction one surveys across their entire national territory. Land surrounds them completely on every side, and such a nation is accordingly designated as landlocked.

A landlocked country possesses no coastline anywhere along its perimeter. It has no port of its own situated by the sea, so large oceangoing vessels can never sail directly to it, simply because it possesses none to sail toward in the first place; every shipment destined for such a nation must instead traverse land, or an inland river system, for a portion of its journey before ever reaching open water.

Landlocked nations exist on nearly every continent of the world. Bolivia and Paraguay sit landlocked in South America, hemmed in by other sovereign nations on every side. Switzerland and Austria are landlocked among the towering mountains of Europe, alongside more than a dozen smaller nations distributed further eastward across that continent. Mongolia is landlocked in Asia, wedged tightly between its two colossal neighbors, Russia and China. Chad, Niger, and Mali are landlocked deep within the interior of Africa, hundreds of kilometers removed from any ocean. A rare handful of nations, including Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan, are classified as doubly landlocked, signifying that every single one of their immediate neighbors is itself landlocked, a geographic coincidence found almost nowhere else on the planet.

In total, approximately 44 countries worldwide are classified as landlocked, identifiable on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, the latter possessing no permanent population or sovereign government whatsoever.

Being landlocked imposes real and persistent economic challenges upon a nation, since large cargo vessels require a coast where they can safely load and unload goods, and in the absence of any coastline of its own, every commodity a landlocked country imports or exports must first transit a neighboring country's sovereign territory, adding both time and considerable extra cost to the final price paid by consumers.

Landlocked nations therefore negotiate detailed transit agreements with their coastal neighbors, under which a neighbor formally permits goods to travel through one of its ports en route to the open sea, while trucks, trains, or river barges convey the cargo the remaining distance across the border.

Switzerland, for instance, ships much of its cargo along the Rhine River to the bustling port of Rotterdam, hundreds of kilometers distant in the Netherlands, while Ethiopia relies heavily upon a modern railway connecting it to a port on the Red Sea. Many landlocked nations also join regional trade organizations, which guarantee member countries a legal right to move goods through a neighbor's territory under agreed, predictable rules rather than fragile, case-by-case negotiation. Trade can thereby continue to flow steadily, even for a nation that possesses no coastline whatsoever of its own.

versions.title: Landlocked Countries: No Coastline
versions.text:
Across the continents of the world, a meticulous examination of a map reveals a boundary line surrounding each sovereign nation, and the overwhelming majority of countries touch the sea along at least a portion of their perimeter, however irregular that coastline might otherwise appear.

Yet a surprising number of countries, scattered across nearly every inhabited continent, do not touch the sea at all, irrespective of which direction one surveys across their entire national territory, since land surrounds them completely on every side, and such a nation is consequently designated as landlocked.

A landlocked country possesses no coastline whatsoever along its perimeter, and it has no port of its own situated by the sea, so large oceangoing vessels can never sail directly to it, simply because it possesses none toward which to navigate in the first place; every shipment destined for such a nation must instead traverse land, or an inland river system, for a considerable portion of its journey before ever reaching open water.

Landlocked nations exist on nearly every continent of the world: Bolivia and Paraguay sit landlocked in South America, hemmed in by other sovereign nations on every side; Switzerland and Austria are landlocked among the towering mountains of Europe, alongside more than a dozen smaller nations distributed further eastward across that continent; Mongolia is landlocked in Asia, wedged tightly between its two colossal neighbors, Russia and China; and Chad, Niger, and Mali are landlocked deep within the interior of Africa, hundreds of kilometers removed from any ocean whatsoever. A rare handful of nations, including Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan, are classified as doubly landlocked, signifying that every single one of their immediate neighbors is itself landlocked, a geographic coincidence found almost nowhere else on the entire planet.

In total, approximately 44 countries worldwide are classified as landlocked, identifiable on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, the latter possessing no permanent population or sovereign government whatsoever.

Being landlocked imposes real and persistent economic challenges upon a nation, since large cargo vessels require a coast where they can safely load and unload merchandise, and in the absence of any coastline of its own, every commodity a landlocked country imports or exports must first transit a neighboring country's sovereign territory, thereby adding both time and considerable extra expense to the final price ultimately paid by consumers throughout the supply chain.

Landlocked nations therefore negotiate detailed transit agreements with their coastal neighbors, under which a neighbor formally permits goods to travel through one of its ports en route to the open sea, while trucks, trains, or river barges convey the merchandise the remaining distance across the border.

Switzerland, for instance, ships much of its cargo along the Rhine River to the bustling port of Rotterdam, hundreds of kilometers distant in the Netherlands, while Ethiopia relies heavily upon a modern railway connecting it to a port on the Red Sea. Many landlocked nations also join regional trade organizations, which guarantee member countries a legal right to move merchandise through a neighbor's territory under agreed, predictable rules rather than fragile, case-by-case negotiation, thereby reducing uncertainty considerably. Trade can thereby continue to flow steadily, even for a nation that possesses no coastline whatsoever of its own.

MID.prompt: Explain two challenges a landlocked country's economy faces, and one way the country can solve each challenge.
checklist: I explained a solution for each challenge.
I used at least two key words from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: One challenge for a landlocked country's economy is that its cargo must pass through a neighbor's border before reaching the sea, and that neighbor can charge fees that raise the cost of trade. A solution is to sign an agreement, which sets clear, agreed rules so goods can move through on a dependable path instead of relying on last-minute deals. A second challenge is that problems with a neighbor can suddenly block a landlocked country's only path to a port. One solution is to use more than one route, such as Switzerland's use of the Rhine River alongside roads and railways, so the country is not dependent on a single crossing.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how a landlocked country can reduce its dependence on a single neighbor for access to the sea. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained at least two ways a country can reduce its dependence on one neighbor.
I used evidence from the article.
I used at least two key words, such as territory or transit.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A landlocked country can reduce its dependence on a single neighbor by building strong transport links, such as a dedicated railway or road, that connect it reliably to a particular port, as Ethiopia has done with its railway to the port of Djibouti. It can also use more than one route rather than relying on only one path to the sea, the way Switzerland moves cargo along the Rhine River while also using roads and railways through several neighboring countries. Finally, joining a regional trade organization gives a landlocked country a guaranteed, predictable right to move goods through member territory, which is far more secure than depending entirely on the goodwill of one sovereign neighbor and the fees or delays it might choose to impose.
